docs.dcterms_abstract: Translation [by Cristina Neagu]: To the prudent and wise gentlemen, Herr Kaspar Nützel, Lazarus Spengler, and Albrecht Dürer, now in Augsburg, our gracious lords and good friends. May Jesus be with you. I wish all the best from the Highest to you, along with my warmest greetings,  gracious lords, good friends, brothers and benefactors. Your friendly letter, and all the news it contained, I received with great joy, read with delight and such devotion, and my eyes more than once filled up with tears, though more of laughter than of emotion. Thank you kindly for your gesture; in your wisdom, engaged in such important affairs of state as you are, and amid such great festivities, you did not forget me, poor little nunlet, and offered me precious guidelines as to how to live an ordered and regulated life; you have such a clear vision of it before your eyes. Without a shadow of a doubt, a good angel has driven you, my gracious lords, to Augsburg, so that you may take example from the free Swabian spirits, on how you ought to instruct and govern us, poor little lambs cloistered on sandy grounds. When our faithful Warden [Kaspar Nützel), enamoured of all things spiritual, has started helping Gründlach convent to reform, he must have looked at the Swabian confederation as to another model of holy observance. Regarding Herr Lazarus Spengler, he should dig deep in search of that special kind of apostolic common life so that he might give counsel and guidance to us and others how to hang about and cash out everything like there is no tomorrow. Finally, Herr Albrecht Dürer (the insightful and ingenious man he is, and ever ready to inspect orderly structures) should we ever decide to remodel our choir, might provide assistance on how to open wide windows, so that our eyes are not entirely strained. To conclude, I shall trouble you no longer to bring us a manuscript from which we could sing from musical notation: our beer is so sour right now, I fear the barrels might burst their four windpipes voice-like spouts, sounding so loudly that dogs might flee off from the church. So, my humble request to you would be as follows : do not strain your eyes too much on the black and white magpies so that you can still recognize the little grey she-wolves of Nuremberg. I have often heard of the clever Swabians, but now I hold them in even greater regard, for they display such  wisdom in their work for his imperial majesty, ensuring that the apostolic life is not disrupted. It is clear they are more steeped into spirituality than our lords here have ever been. Please, my gracious lords, do forgive my ramblings. It’s all done in jest and Christian love. Summing up, I wish you all the best. Return soon, healthy, full of success and the desired results. I, along with the sisters here, pray to God for you, night and day. But we cannot do much alone, so my advice is that you also call upon other devout pure hearts so that they may lift their voices towards heaven to make your dreams come true. My blessing to you all. Given in Nuremberg, on 3 September 1518. S. Caritas, pointless abbess of St. Clare's in Nuremberg.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She cites Scripture, which she feels compels her, even as a woman, to speak out against the university's proceedings against Arsacius Seehofer. She condemns his violent imprisonment and the threat of execution which they used to force him to recant Lutheran teachings, especially in view of his young age. In her view, Luther and Melanchthon have taught no heresy and  to deny them would be to deny God. She criticizes those who preach against heresy without explaining which articles are meant to be heretical. She believes that the university has neglected Scripture, given too much deference to the Roman Church, and been driven by greed to mislead the princes. If the princes were told the truth, she believes they would revoke the university's authority to employ the kind of force they used against Seehofer. 
Both Jesus and Jerome were not ashamed to teach women and this emboldens her to ask questions and understand answers. Her letter is not just woman's talk, but the word of God proclaimed to the university by a fellow member of the Christian Church.

She describes how the young Arsacius Seehofer, after imprisonment and under the threat of death, was forced to deny all of Luther's writings. As, in her view, all Luther has done is translate the Bible into German, this is akin to being forced to deny the Gospel. She believes Wilhelm must have been misinformed when he allowed this to happen. 
She appeals to him to test everything he is told by the Spirit according to the Scripture. He should take care not to misuse his authority, as this will be avenged by God, nor allow himself to be led astray by the nuns, monks, and priests, whom she accuses of greed and theft and the maintenance of prostitutes. If religious institutions paid taxes and were not populated by absentee benefit-holders, she argues, Wilhelm could use it to defend against the Turks and benefit the poor. 
She writes to him as a brother, father, and neighbour in Christ, because of his kindness to her after her parents' death and his generosity to her husband. It was her duty as a Christian to write to the university, which letter she encloses in order that he may be fully informed.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She recently wrote to the University of Ingolstadt regarding Seehofer and, though she expected them to keep the matter private and point out errors to her personally, it has become public. She has been accosted by many people and sends the council a copy of her letter in order that she may not be misinterpreted. 
She is confident that the Spirit of God will judge her properly and protect her from the death threats that she has faced. She appeals to their shared baptismal vow which calls them to renounce illusions of the devil. No amount of theological study will make someone else's baptismal vow worth more than hers. She compares the behaviour of the 'sophists' at Ingolstadt to the Jews who rejected Jesus. 
Even if she were murdered, she believes a hundred women would rise and continue her writing, even better than she could. Yet she rejoices in her persecution for the sake of the Gospel. She cites Scripture encouraging the council to resist the clergy's false teaching lest they perish alongside them, and asks them to pray for her as she prays for them.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She knows that he has learned of her letter to the university and is angry at her. She concludes that someone who did not wish her well would not pay attention to gossip about her, and sends a copy of her letter with an appeal to judge her in the Spirit. While she will endure punishment for error, she will not be criticized for fulfilling her baptismal vows, which are as great as any prince or pope's. In her view, her confession of God is a confirmation of her faith as a Christian. She confesses Christ, in whom she was baptized, and not Luther, though she confesses that Luther is a faithful Christian. 
Reports that her husband is not walling her up are misguided, as he is doing 'far too much'. Yet she endures this too and is confident that in this matter she is not obligated to obey her husband. She is disappointed at the princes' ignorance of the word of God and moral deprivation around her, particularly faithlessness in marriage. She expects little of the next Reichstag after witnessing the 'childish' behaviour of the princes at the last one. 
She appeals to Thering to read the whole Bible, as he is in a position to appoint good preachers in his territory. Though she has heard that her husband will be dismissed from office, she has weighed this possibility and is prepared to lose everything. She is confident that God will care for her children and that it is the will of God that her writing be public, despite her initial wish for privacy.

docs.dcterms_abstract: She addresses the council as brothers in Christ and expresses distress at an edict in Regensburg which she believes is being promulgated under Satan's initiative. She urges them to read the Scripture about the end times and recognize that they are under the power of Satan, whom she connects with the Pope. She is compelled by her duty as a fellow Christian to write to them, even though she knows it will engender derision. She urges them to be mindful of their duty to the souls of others, to resist the distraction of tradition, and to fight against the enemies of God. Yet this fight should only use the word of God as a weapon and people should continue to live peacefully with each other. She knows that, like Paul, she will be dismissed as weak and foolish, but this does not matter to her.

docs.dcterms_abstract: She is writing about the vicar Jakob Pfeffer in the Parish of Zeilitzheim, who has resigned his position. Argula's brother-in-law Frederick von Leonrod (the canon of Eichstätt) and her husband are considering employing someone else. On their instructions she has written this to Pfeffer. She encloses a letter from Frederick about the matter and assures Geys von Hesperck that she is committed to ensuring a fair resolution of the situation. She will send a letter carrier to receive his reply quickly, and further notes that her husband has heard accounts of Pfeffer's trickery.

docs.dcterms_abstract: She was shocked to learn through his letter what happened at Burggrumbach, and expresses deep hurt at her children's disobedience. As he has asked for her forgiveness, she urges him to come home after taking the sacrament at Nuremberg. He is to confess everything to Osiander and bring written confirmation of having received the sacrament, but he must keep the matter secret from everyone else. He must also bring an itemized account of his debts to his landlord in Nuremberg and commend obedience and discipline to his younger brother Gottfried. A note on the letter indicates the matter in question was related to the son of Claus Manger.
